audit-purpose-analysis.title: What Is a Safety Audit and Workplace Analysis
audit-purpose-analysis.content: A safety audit is an organized examination of the workplace to determine how safe it is and what can be improved. Its purpose is to identify unsafe conditions and practices, evaluate existing controls, check emergency readiness, and support corrective action before accidents occur — not to find someone to blame. A good audit looks at work areas, equipment, tools, procedures, emergency systems, employee training, PPE, and hazard reporting. Workplace analysis is a core part of every audit: a careful, regular review of the jobsite, work areas, equipment, materials, procedures, and employee activities. Conditions that were safe last month may not be safe today — new equipment, changed processes, modified procedures, or employee shortcuts can all introduce new hazards. Employees play an essential role because they use the tools, operate the equipment, follow the procedures, and often recognize hazards before anyone else does.

controls-overview.title: The System of Controls: Administrative, Engineering, and PPE
controls-overview.content: Safety audits must evaluate the complete system of controls used to protect workers. Administrative controls are rules, policies, procedures, schedules, and work practices designed to reduce risk — examples include no-smoking policies, permit systems, warning signs, and job rotation. These controls are only effective when clearly written, communicated, understood, and followed. Engineering controls are physical safeguards built into the workplace, tools, equipment, or processes — examples include machine guards, ventilation systems, guardrails, interlocks, noise enclosures, and barriers. They are often more reliable than rules because they reduce the hazard at its source. PPE — safety glasses, gloves, hard hats, face shields, respirators, hearing protection — is used when other controls cannot fully eliminate a hazard. PPE must be selected for the specific hazard, inspected before every use, worn correctly, and replaced when damaged. Damaged or wrong-type PPE provides little or no protection even when worn.

tools-machinery.title: Tools, Machinery, and Equipment Maintenance
tools-machinery.content: Tools and machinery are major audit focus areas. Equipment that is worn out, damaged, poorly maintained, set up incorrectly, or modified unsafely can create serious hazards. Auditors should look for missing guards, damaged cords, leaks, worn parts, improper setups, unauthorized modifications, and evidence that maintenance is being skipped. A machine guard that has been removed to speed up work is a critical safety defect — the machine should be taken out of service and the guard reinstalled before anyone uses it again. A damaged extension cord with cracked insulation must be removed from service immediately. Every worker has a responsibility to report equipment hazards as soon as they are discovered, and defective equipment must not be used until repaired or replaced. A good maintenance program ensures defective equipment is corrected before it causes an accident.

emergency-response.title: Emergency Response Procedures
emergency-response.content: Even workplaces with strong safety programs can experience accidents and emergencies. Safety audits must verify that emergency response systems are in place and ready. During an audit, check whether emergency phone numbers are posted, exits are clear and properly marked, emergency lighting functions, fire extinguishers are accessible, first aid kits are fully stocked, eyewash stations and safety showers are available where needed, and employees know how to report an emergency. Emergency equipment must never be blocked — in an emergency, every second counts. Employees should only use emergency equipment such as fire extinguishers if they have been trained and authorized to do so. A blocked fire extinguisher or cluttered exit route found during an audit must be corrected immediately, and storage rules must be reviewed to prevent recurrence.

incident-reporting.title: Medical Programs, Injury Trends, and Near-Miss Reporting
incident-reporting.content: Safety audits should review how the facility handles injuries, illnesses, accident reporting, and accident investigation. When an injury occurs, medical care is the first priority. After care, the incident must be documented and investigated to find causes and prevent recurrence. Accident investigation should never be used to assign blame — its purpose is to determine what happened, why, and how to prevent it. Audits can reveal injury patterns: if several workers are injured on the same machine or during the same task, that pattern points to a hazard requiring correction. Near misses are equally important. A near miss is an incident that could have caused injury under slightly different circumstances — it is a warning. Reporting near misses allows the workplace to correct hazards before someone gets hurt. Unreported near misses represent missed opportunities for prevention.

training-self-assessment.title: Safety Training and Employee Self-Assessment
training-self-assessment.content: Training is one of the most important elements of a strong safety program. An audit should evaluate whether employees have received required training, whether they understand it, and whether they apply it on the job. Training topics may include PPE, emergency procedures, hazard reporting, housekeeping, hazard communication, lockout/tagout, process safety, and job-specific requirements. Training must be updated when equipment changes, procedures change, or new hazards are introduced. Employees can also conduct a personal safety self-assessment: a review of their own work habits, knowledge of workplace hazards, and emergency readiness. Self-assessment questions include: Do I follow standard operating procedures every time? Do I ever skip a step to save time? Do I inspect my PPE before using it? Do I know the location of emergency exits, fire extinguishers, eyewash stations, and first aid kits? Taking responsibility for personal safety knowledge supports both individual and team safety.

corrective-actions.title: Corrective Actions and Continuous Improvement
corrective-actions.content: Finding a hazard is only the first step — a safety audit is effective only when hazards are corrected. Corrective actions may include repairing equipment, changing procedures, improving training, increasing supervision, updating PPE, improving signage, clearing access routes, or redesigning work processes. Every corrective action should be documented, assigned to a responsible person, tracked, and verified as completed. Audits should not be one-time events. They are part of continuous improvement: as work changes, safety systems must be regularly reviewed and strengthened. Employees support continuous improvement by reporting hazards promptly, suggesting improvements, and consistently following safe work practices. In hazardous materials and process safety environments, timely follow-up on audit findings is especially critical because uncontrolled hazards can have serious consequences.

options.text: To identify and discipline employees who violate safety rules
To identify hazards and correct them before injuries occur
To prepare documentation for an upcoming OSHA visit
To compare safety performance across competing facilities

options.text: Identifying and evaluating hazards in the work environment
Calculating the cost of workplace injuries
Determining which employees need disciplinary action
Reviewing production output against safety benchmarks

3.questionText: Which of the following best describes an administrative control?

options.text: Installing a physical guard on a machine
Providing chemical-resistant gloves to employees
Adding an exhaust ventilation system
Establishing a written policy prohibiting smoking near flammable materials

4.questionText: An engineering control is best described as:

options.text: A policy requiring employees to follow safety procedures
A physical modification to the workplace, equipment, or process that reduces hazard exposure
Personal protective equipment selected for a specific hazard
A training program designed to improve employee awareness

options.text: Once per month
Once per year
Only after an incident
Before each use
